transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-09-14 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Nina Patel (Redwood SE), Maria Gomez (Sapphire - Head of Data), Ethan Brooks (Sapphire - Platform Engineer), Priya Singh (Sapphire - Security)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to validate Sapphire's embedding scale and hosting constraints; main asks: throughput to support 200 QPS at 1k doc fanout, durability for PHI-ish metadata, and ability to run on a private VPC.

Topics flagged: embedding dims, quantization tradeoffs, rerank vs vector-fanout latency, dedicated vs hosted, SOC2/KMS, pilot benchmarks.

00:00:10 Liam (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we wanted to run through your embedding pipeline and what you're trying to accomplish, and then we'll talk hosting options and performance.
00:00:23 Maria (Sapphire): Thanks Liam, appreciate it. Quick context, we ingest clinical notes and some patient-reported outcomes. Not full PHI in many cases but some fields are sensitive so we need encryption at rest and audit logs.
00:00:38 Liam: Totally, yeah that's super common. Nina will do the deep technical stuff but first maybe you can sketch the current pipeline?
00:00:45 Ethan: Sure, so currently we use an in-house embedder (custom 1536-d vectors) then store vectors in Redis for fast recall. We do a light rerank with a small cross-encoder, but that is the bottleneck. We're exploring moving to a two-stage approach: fast vector fanout for topk then rerank using a Redwood hosted model or on-prem model.
00:01:10 Nina (Redwood SE): Okay, couple clarifying q's — when you say 1536-d, are those float32 or have you experimented with lower precision / quant?
00:01:18 Ethan: Right now float32, not quantized. We've looked at int8 but saw losses in relevance for certain clinical terms.
00:01:27 Nina: Got it. Two patterns we typically see: 1) full fanout where you compute embedding similarity topk from the VDB and then do a small rerank on the top 50-200; or 2) hybrid routing where a lightweight scoring model runs first and we only call a heavier re-ranker for ambiguous queries. Both have tradeoffs in tail latency and cost.
00:01:52 Maria: We care about tail latency — anything above 300ms for the first result is noticeable in the UI.
00:01:58 Liam: Understood, and rough QPS?
00:02:02 Maria: Spiky, but baseline 30 qps with peaks to 200 qps during batch uploads or clinician hours.
00:02:10 Nina: OK, so you'd likely be looking at batching and dedicated capacity. For dedicated we can keep hot KV caches and pre-warmed models to hit lower tail latencies.
00:02:22 Ethan: When you say KV cache, do you mean Redwood's prefix/K V cache? I saw that in docs but sometimes the transcription has it as K V cache.
00:02:31 Nina: Yep, KV cache — sorry sometimes the auto-titles get weird — it's the model key-value attention cache for repeated sessions but we also do prefix caching for common queries which helps.

00:03:05 Liam: Let's dive into the hosting modes briefly: hosted API is easiest to start and we offer embeddings + rerank endpoints. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools so you get predictable throughput and slightly lower per-token cost. Private (VPC/on-prem) isolates control plane and networking for compliance. Which of these are you leaning to?
00:03:26 Maria: Private would be ideal due to compliance, but we want to understand cost delta and the effort to deploy.
00:03:34 Liam: Right. For Private you'll manage the network, and we integrate with your KMS/HSM for key management. There's extra setup (helm charts or infra templates), and we provide an on-prem package if you're fully air-gapped.
00:03:49 Priya (Security): Quick question — do you have SOC 2 reports and can we see your KMS integration docs? Also, how do you handle audit logs and deletion requests?
00:03:59 Liam: Yes, we can share SOC 2 and our KMS integration docs. Audit logs include per-request traces and token-level cost breakdowns; deletion requests are supported and we have retention configs. We'll drop the docs in the follow-up.

00:04:30 Nina: Back to throughput — you mentioned 200 QPS peaks with 1k doc fanout. If you're doing naive fanout and rerank that would be expensive. Typical engineering pattern is to reduce vector dims, quantize embeddings (e.g., 256 or 512 compact embeddings with PQ or product quant), and run approximate topk search with a vector DB shard topology to get top 100 then rerank. That usually keeps rerank calls to under 30 per query.
00:04:59 Ethan: If we go to 512 dims with int8 or 4-bit quant, how much relevance drop are we likely to see for clinical terms?
00:05:07 Nina: It depends on your eval set. Our Optimize tooling can suggest quantization profiles per workload. In past med datasets, 512 with 8-bit often preserves most signal; 4-bit can be risky for edge cases. We also recommend a retrain or calibration step for sensitive token distributions.
00:05:28 Maria: We do have an internal eval set — about 10k labeled queries. Could you run a quick benchmark?
00:05:34 Nina: Yes, that's exactly what we do in pilots — we run a rerank A/B using your eval queries and measure MRR/recall and tail latency. For a pilot we typically spin up a dedicated pool for 48-72h.

00:06:10 Liam: On the integration front, do you prefer using a Vector DB as the primary store or Redwood as the embedding store with synchronous writes to the VDB?
00:06:18 Ethan: Today we keep embeddings in Redis; for benchmarks we'd be open to experimenting with both a managed VDB and our current Redis to compare.
00:06:26 Nina: Totally reasonable. We commonly integrate with managed VDBs (Pinecone, Milvus, RedisVector) and also with in-cluster systems. For high QPS, sharding the index and having coordinated fanout can reduce per-node load. We'll test both approaches in the pilot.

00:07:05 Maria: Side note — are there options for on-demand quantization conversion? i.e., store full floats but serve quantized vectors for inference?
00:07:13 Nina: Yes, that pattern works well. Keep base store as float32 for retraining/analytics and maintain a quantized replica for serving. Redwood supports caching of quantized variants and we can wire automated conversion in the pipeline.

00:07:45 Liam: Let's talk numbers — what would dedicated capacity look like to cover 200 QPS with our fanout targets? Nina, do you have a rough estimate?
00:07:54 Nina: Ballpark: if you're aiming for top-k 100 then a small rerank model (~1B) on a dedicated A100-class node with batching tuned could handle sustained 100 qps per node with low tail latency; for peaks to 200 you'd want 2-3 nodes with autoscaling/burst. Embedding lookups are much cheaper — those scale horizontally in the vector DB. Exact numbers depend on sequence length and model size.
00:08:20 Ethan: Our current reranker is 350m parameters, but we were exploring replacing it with an L2-based lightweight model or Redwood's hosted small re-ranker.
00:08:30 Nina: If you can keep reranker small, you can get great latency. Also consider offloading some work to cached prefix scores for very common queries.

00:09:05 Priya: About keys — KMS integration, do you support customer-managed keys across Hosted and Dedicated?
00:09:12 Liam: For Hosted we offer integration with major cloud KMS providers and we can support customer-managed keys; for Dedicated and Private you have full control — you bring your KMS/HSM and we integrate.
00:09:24 Priya: Good. Also need SSO/SAML and RBAC.
00:09:28 Liam: We support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and role-based access controls; we'll include those in the security packet.

00:10:02 Maria: On the dataset for the pilot, if we provide 10k labeled queries and a 1M doc index, is that sufficient?
00:10:10 Nina: Yes, that's a good starting point. For throughput tests we'd want a synthetic workload to simulate peaks and also real queries to test relevance.
00:10:18 Ethan: For indexing, we might batch- ingest monthly, so ingestion throughput matters as well — say 100k embeddings per hour during re-index windows.
00:10:28 Nina: Dedicated pools can be tuned for ingest throughput as well; we can advise on sharding strategies and backpressure.

00:11:00 Liam: Any blockers on compliance that would prevent a Private deployment?
00:11:05 Priya: Data residency is one: we need EU-resident instances for certain datasets. Also, auditability from our security team — they want to see per-request cryptographic signatures if possible.
00:11:18 Liam: We do region pinning and can set up EU-hosted private deployment. For signatures we can add request-level metadata and integrate with your SIEM.

00:11:45 Maria: Are there customers in healthcare using Private already?
00:11:48 Liam: Yes, a couple. We can anonymize examples and include high-level architecture diagrams in the follow-up.

00:12:15 Nina: Quick note on hybrid search: sometimes we do a small model embed on the client side to reduce cross-traffic, then a server-side heavier rerank — saves cost. But that requires trust on the client side and increases client complexity.
00:12:29 Ethan: Might be ok for internal clinician apps but not external patient-facing.

00:13:00 Maria: Let's talk evals — can Redwood run an MRR/Precision@k baseline for our 10k queries with both 1536 and compact 512 configs?
00:13:08 Nina: Yes, we'll run A/B: 1536 float32 baseline, 512 int8, and 256 with PQ and report MRR/recall + latency. We also instrument per-query failures.

00:13:40 Liam: For billing — hosted is usage-based, dedicated is reserved monthly pricing with committed capacity, private has licensing and support fees. We'll share a pricing matrix.
00:13:53 Maria: For the pilot, we're interested in a short-term dedicated pool rather than hosted to get deterministic latency.
00:13:59 Liam: That makes sense for your tail SLOs. We can propose a 4-week pilot with dedicated nodes.

00:14:30 Ethan: One technical nit — how do you handle model rollouts and fallback? Suppose a rerank deploy regresses, can we automatically fallback to prior model?
00:14:39 Nina: Yes, Redwood supports rollouts with canary and automatic fallback policies. You can pin model versions and split traffic for A/B. We also have quality monitoring tied to prompts/eval sets to detect regressions.

00:15:05 Maria: Do you capture token-level cost so we can attribute costs to features?
00:15:10 Liam: Yes, token-level cost and per-route breakdown is in Redwood Console.

00:15:40 Liam: Anything else on infra?
00:15:42 Ethan: If we wanted to experiment with vector-db-less flow — storing embeddings in Redwood-managed store and doing the similarity on the runtime — is that on the roadmap?
00:15:53 Nina: We have an internal experimental feature for that but for production we recommend a dedicated VDB for scale. For small indices it's feasible to serve directly but not at your 1M docs target.

00:16:25 Maria: Are there any known gotchas for clinical synonyms and OOV tokens when you quantize?
00:16:31 Nina: OOV can hurt with heavy quant; calibration and re-embedding frequent terms helps. Also consider a hybrid representation where you keep subword-level signals for medical nomenclature.

00:17:00 Priya: On audit logs — retention policy and who can access?
00:17:05 Liam: Retention is configurable per-customer; access controlled via RBAC, and logs can be pushed to your SIEM.

00:17:40 Ethan: For the pilot metrics, can we define SLOs: p95 latency under 300ms for top1 on clinician UI, and throughput sustain at 150 qps with spikes to 200?
00:17:51 Nina: Yes, we can set those SLOs and measure in the smoke test. We'll include dashboards and tracing hooks.

00:18:25 Maria: Regarding privacy, if an embed contains sensitive tokens, is there a way to redact fields before embedding?
00:18:33 Liam: Yes, pre-processing to remove PHI is recommended; we also support per-field hashing or tokenization before embedding.

00:19:00 Ethan: About latency budget: when we do fanout->rerank, what's the expected added time per rerank call?
00:19:07 Nina: If reranker is small (300-600m) and on dedicated node with batching, per-call can be 20-60ms depending on batching. But end-to-end includes VDB lookup, network, so more like 80-200ms.

00:19:45 Maria: Any recommended vector DB for our use-case?
00:19:50 Nina: For high QPS and low latency, enterprise RedisVector or sharded Milvus works well. Pinecone is great for managed ease but watch shard limits. We'll share benchmark references.

00:20:20 Liam: Let's capture concrete next steps — we'll run a pilot: 48-72h dedicated run, evaluate embedding dims (1536 vs 512 vs 256 PQ), compare VDB integration (RedisVector vs managed), and produce MRR/latency numbers. We'll also send SOC2/KMS docs.

00:20:45 Maria: Sounds good. For scheduling, how quickly can we start?
00:20:48 Liam: If you approve the pilot SOW, we can stand up dedicated nodes in 5–7 business days.

00:21:10 Ethan: On dataset transfer for the pilot, is S3 acceptable?
00:21:14 Nina: Yes, S3 or signed uploads; for private deployments we can also set up direct transfer into your VPC.

00:21:40 Priya: We'll need to check legal on the SOW and data transfer, but security looks promising so far.

00:22:05 Liam: Any final questions from the Sapphire team?
00:22:10 Maria: Not right now. We'll consolidate questions and send them to Liam.

[short pause — meeting moves toward close]

00:23:00 Liam: Great — to recap: action items (we'll put in the notes) — pricing + SOW from Liam; smoke-test plan from Nina; security checklist from Priya. We'll plan a kickoff for the pilot once SOW is approved.
00:23:22 Maria: Thank you, appreciate it.
00:23:25 Ethan: Thanks all.
00:23:28 Nina: Thanks, bye.
